target_skill: Determine gamete chromosome numbers after a specific nondisjunction event in meiosis and combine them into a requested numeric quantity.
novel_context: Pollen formation in a fictional flowering plant species with a single nondisjunction event in meiosis I and a non-standard numerical request (product of chromosome counts across all resulting gametes).
fixed_givens: You are studying meiosis in a fictional flowering plant species.
In this species, somatic (body) cells are diploid with 2n = 10 chromosomes.
You observe meiosis in a single diploid cell that will form pollen grains (male gametes).
During meiosis I in this cell, exactly one pair of homologous chromosomes fails to separate (a nondisjunction event).
All other homologous chromosome pairs separate normally in meiosis I.
During meiosis II, all chromosomes (including any that were affected by the meiosis I error) separate normally; there are no additional nondisjunction events.
Assume that each completed meiosis from this cell produces exactly four pollen grains (gametes), as usual.
Chromosome counts are always reported as numbers of chromosomes per cell, not chromatids.

Question to answer: After this one meiosis with the described nondisjunction in meiosis I, what is the product of the chromosome numbers in all four resulting pollen grains? (Multiply the chromosome numbers of the four gametes together to get a single integer.)

nodes.label: Diploid somatic cells of the plant species have 2n = 10 chromosomes.
The haploid chromosome number is n = 10 / 2 = 5 in normal gametes.
Exactly one homologous chromosome pair fails to separate in meiosis I (nondisjunction), while all other pairs separate normally.
In meiosis I nondisjunction of one homologous pair, both homologs of that pair go to the same pole; no gamete receives exactly one chromosome from that pair.

After meiosis I with nondisjunction of one pair, one daughter cell receives both homologs of the affected pair (2 from that pair), and the other daughter receives none (0 from that pair); all other pairs are split 1-and-1.
Counting all chromosomes, one meiosis I daughter cell has (n + 1) = 5 + 1 = 6 chromosomes; the other has (n − 1) = 5 − 1 = 4 chromosomes.
In meiosis II with normal separation of sister chromatids, each meiosis I daughter cell produces two gametes that share its chromosome count (no further gain or loss of whole chromosomes).
The meiosis I daughter with 6 chromosomes produces two gametes with 6 chromosomes each; the meiosis I daughter with 4 chromosomes produces two gametes with 4 chromosomes each.
Compute the product of the chromosome numbers of all four gametes: (6) × (6) × (4) × (4).

verification.expected_answer: The four gametes have chromosome numbers 6, 6, 4, and 4; their product is 576.
verification.calculation: From 2n = 10, the haploid number is n = 5. A meiosis I nondisjunction of one homologous pair gives one meiosis I daughter cell with n + 1 = 6 chromosomes and the other with n − 1 = 4 chromosomes, with all other pairs behaving normally. Each of these cells undergoes normal meiosis II, so the 6-chromosome cell produces two gametes with 6 chromosomes each, and the 4-chromosome cell produces two gametes with 4 chromosomes each. The requested product of the chromosome numbers is 6 × 6 × 4 × 4 = 576.

distractor_mechanisms: Assume the nondisjunction happens in meiosis II instead of meiosis I, leading to an incorrect 5, 5, 6, 4 set of gamete chromosome numbers and a wrong product.
Confuse chromosome number with chromatid number, doubling counts (e.g., treating the diploid as 20 and deriving incorrect gamete chromosome numbers).
Forget that n = 2n/2 and treat 2n = 10 as if gametes normally had 10 chromosomes, giving products like 11 × 11 × 9 × 9 or 10 × 10 × 10 × 10.

target_skill: Use a Punnett square to compute the probability of a dominant phenotype from a heterozygous × homozygous recessive monohybrid cross.
novel_context: Flower color in a fictional plant species (starflowers) controlled by a single gene with complete dominance.
prompt: In starflowers, purple petals are controlled by a dominant allele P, and white petals are controlled by a recessive allele p. A plant that is heterozygous purple (Pp) is crossed with a white plant (pp). What fraction of their offspring are expected to have purple petals?
fixed_givens: Species: starflower (fictional plant).
Trait of interest: petal color.
Single gene with two alleles controls this trait: P and p.
P (purple) is completely dominant to p (white).
Genotypes and phenotypes: PP = purple, Pp = purple, pp = white.
Cross: Parent 1 genotype Pp (heterozygous purple) × Parent 2 genotype pp (homozygous white).
Assume standard Mendelian inheritance with equal segregation of alleles and no linkage or other complicating factors.
Question: Determine the fraction (probability) of offspring that will have purple petals.

nodes.label: Alleles: P and p; P is dominant (purple), p is recessive (white).
Parent 1 genotype: Pp (heterozygous purple).
Parent 2 genotype: pp (homozygous white).
Mendel’s law of segregation: each parent contributes one of its two alleles to each offspring with equal probability.
Possible gametes from Parent 1 (Pp): P or p, each with probability 1/2.
Possible gametes from Parent 2 (pp): only p gametes (probability 1 for allele p).
Offspring genotypes from combining gametes: 1/2 Pp (P from Parent 1, p from Parent 2) and 1/2 pp (p from Parent 1, p from Parent 2).
Phenotypes: Pp is purple, pp is white.
Fraction of offspring with purple petals is 1/2.
Assume any presence of recessive allele p makes the flower white, leading to 0 purple offspring.
Treat Pp × pp as if both parents were heterozygous (Pp × Pp), giving 3/4 purple offspring.
Confuse genotype ratio (1:1) with fraction of dominant phenotype and answer 1/4 instead of 1/2.

verification.expected_answer: 1/2 of the offspring will have purple petals (choice C: 1/2).
verification.calculation: Parent 1 (Pp) produces P and p gametes in equal proportion: P = 1/2, p = 1/2. Parent 2 (pp) produces only p gametes: p = 1. Combining: probability of Pp = (1/2)*1 = 1/2, probability of pp = (1/2)*1 = 1/2. Only genotypes with at least one P are purple, so fraction purple = 1/2 = 0.5.

distractor_mechanisms: Assume that any genotype with a recessive allele p is white, ignoring dominance (leads to choosing 0).
Mistakenly treat the cross as Pp × Pp and apply the 3/4 dominant phenotype rule from a monohybrid self-cross (leads to choosing 3/4).
Confuse the 1:1 genotype ratio with a quarter fraction or miscount possibilities, leading to 1/4 as the answer.

target_skill: Use incomplete dominance and conditional probability to compute genotype and phenotype probabilities from a monohybrid cross
novel_context: Flower color in a fictional plant species where heterozygotes show an intermediate phenotype (incomplete dominance), and students must find the probability of a phenotype given that another phenotype class is excluded
fixed_givens: In a fictional plant called skyflower, petal color is controlled by a single gene with two alleles: B and W.
The gene shows incomplete dominance:
— Genotype BB produces dark blue petals.
— Genotype BW produces light blue petals.
— Genotype WW produces white petals.
Two light blue skyflower plants are crossed.
Assume each parent is genotype BW and that alleles segregate normally during meiosis.

Question: If you randomly select one offspring from this cross and you are told that the offspring is NOT white, what is the probability that this offspring has dark blue petals? Give your answer as a simplified fraction or decimal.

nodes.label: Single gene with two alleles (B and W) shows incomplete dominance: BB = dark blue, BW = light blue, WW = white.
Both parents are light blue, so each parent has genotype BW.
Mendelian segregation for this gene: each parent contributes one allele (B or W) at random to each offspring.
Possible offspring genotypes from BW × BW and their basic probabilities: BB, BW, BW, WW → 1/4 BB, 1/2 BW, 1/4 WW.
Corresponding phenotype probabilities before any condition: dark blue (BB) = 1/4, light blue (BW) = 1/2, white (WW) = 1/4.
Condition: the chosen offspring is NOT white, so WW offspring are excluded.
Total probability of non-white offspring = P(BB) + P(BW) = 1/4 + 1/2 = 3/4.
Conditional probability that the offspring is dark blue (BB) given it is not white: P(BB | not WW).
Conditional probability rule: P(A | B) = P(A and B) / P(B). Here, A = dark blue (BB), B = not white.
Because all BB offspring are non-white, P(BB and not WW) = P(BB) = 1/4.
Compute P(BB | not WW) = (1/4) ÷ (3/4) = 1/3.

verification.calculation: From BW × BW, genotype probabilities are 1/4 BB, 1/2 BW, 1/4 WW. Phenotypes: dark blue = 1/4, light blue = 1/2, white = 1/4. Non-white offspring are BB or BW with total probability 1/4 + 1/2 = 3/4. All BB offspring are non-white, so P(BB and non-white) = 1/4. Using conditional probability, P(dark blue | not white) = (1/4) ÷ (3/4) = 1/3.

distractor_mechanisms: Ignore the conditional information and answer 1/4, using the unconditional probability of dark blue offspring from BW × BW.
Correctly find the non-white probability as 3/4 but then mistakenly report 3/4 instead of 1/3, confusing P(non-white) with P(dark blue | non-white).
Treat the trait as if it showed complete dominance (e.g., lumping BB and BW as the same phenotype) and miscount phenotypes, leading to an incorrect conditional ratio such as 1/2.
